title: Reverse Linked List
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the new head. You must change the next pointers, not just the values.
example: Explanation: Every arrow now points the opposite way; the old tail is the new head.
intuition: Each node only knows its successor. To reverse, every node must point to its predecessor instead. While walking forward we can remember the previous node in a variable prev. The only danger is that when we overwrite curr.next = prev, we lose the way forward, so we save next = curr.next first.

Trace on 1 -> 2 -> 3: start prev = null, curr = 1. Save next = 2, set 1.next = null, move prev = 1, curr = 2. Save next = 3, set 2.next = 1, move on. Set 3.next = 2. curr becomes null, and prev = 3 is the new head.
notes: Say it like this: "The simple way is to copy values into a stack and write them back, O(n) time and O(n) space, but that changes values, not links. The proper way is to walk once with prev, curr and next pointers and flip each arrow, O(n) time and O(1) space. Recursion also works but uses O(n) call stack."
Edge cases: empty list (return null), single node.
Common mistakes: forgetting to save next before flipping; returning head or curr instead of prev; in recursion, forgetting head.next = null (creates a 2-node cycle).
Follow-ups: "Reverse between positions left and right" (LeetCode 92): walk to the node before left, reverse right-left+1 nodes, reconnect both ends. "Reverse in groups of k": see 5.11. 5.2
simple: Make a linked list point the other way round.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Walk the list and push every value onto a stack (or array).
Walk the list again and overwrite each node's value with the popped value.
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the stack holds all n values. (It also cheats by swapping values instead of links, which interviewers may not accept.)
approaches.simple: Read all values into a stack, then write them back in reverse order.

approaches.label: Optimal (Iterative Three Pointers)
steps: prev = null, curr = head.
While curr!= null: save next = curr.next, point curr.next = prev, then prev = curr, curr = next.
Return prev.
approaches.why: One pass over the list; only three pointer variables regardless of n.
extra: A recursive version is also common: reverse head.next recursively, then head.next.next = head; head.next = null. It is O(n) time but O(n) stack space.
approaches.simple: Walk the list with three pointers: remember the next node, flip the current arrow back to the previous node, then step forward.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problem: You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists. Merge them into one sorted list by splicing together the existing nodes, and return its head.
example: Explanation: Repeatedly take the smaller front node of the two lists.
intuition: This is the merge step of merge sort. At any moment the smallest remaining element is at the front of one of the two lists, so compare the two fronts, attach the smaller one to the result, and advance in that list. When one list runs out, the other list is already sorted, so attach it whole.
The head of the result is not known in advance (could come from either list). A dummy node solves this: we always append to tail.next, and at the end return dummy.next.
notes: Say it like this: "I could dump both lists into an array and sort, O((n+m) log(n+m)). Since both are already sorted, I merge them like merge sort: compare the fronts, attach the smaller to a dummy-headed result, and attach the leftover at the end. That is O(n+m) time and O(1) extra space."
Edge cases: one or both lists empty; lists of very different lengths; duplicates across lists.
Common mistakes: forgetting to attach the leftover; forgetting to advance tail; returning dummy instead of dummy.next.
Follow-ups: Recursive version (if l1.val <= l2.val: l1.next = merge(l1.next, l2); return l1) is elegant but uses O(n+m) stack. Merge k lists: see 5.10. 5.3
simple: Join two sorted linked lists into one sorted list.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Copy all values of both lists into an array.
Sort the array.
Build a new linked list from the sorted array.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the array and new nodes take linear space. It ignores that inputs are already sorted.
approaches.simple: Copy all values into an array, sort, and build a new list.

approaches.label: Optimal (Iterative Merge with Dummy)
steps: Create dummy, set tail = dummy.
While both lists are non-empty, attach the smaller front node to tail.next, advance that list and tail.
Attach whichever list is left over. Return dummy.next.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; we only relink existing nodes, using a constant number of pointers.
approaches.simple: Start from a dummy node. Repeatedly attach whichever front node is smaller, then attach the leftovers.

title: Linked List Cycle
problem: Given the head of a linked list, return true if some node can be reached again by following next pointers (the list has a cycle), otherwise false.
example: Input:    head = 3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4, and -4.next points back to the node 2
Explanation: Following next from -4 returns to 2, so we loop forever.
intuition: If there is no cycle, walking the list eventually hits null. If there is a cycle, we walk forever, so we need a way to notice we are going round in circles.

Option one: remember every node we have seen; seeing a node twice means a cycle. Option two (no memory): run two pointers, slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps. Without a cycle, fast hits null. With a cycle, once both are inside the loop, the gap between them shrinks by exactly 1 per step, so fast must land on slow; it can never "jump over" it.
notes: Say it like this: "A hash set of visited nodes detects a repeat in O(n) time and O(n) space. Floyd's algorithm does it in O(1) space: slow moves one step, fast two; if there's a cycle the gap shrinks by one each step so they must meet, otherwise fast reaches null."
Edge cases: empty list; single node without cycle; single node pointing to itself (cycle).
Common mistakes: comparing values instead of node references; checking slow == fast before moving (they start equal); not checking fast.next before fast.next.next.

Follow-ups: "Where does the cycle start?" (5.15). "How long is the cycle?" (5.16). "Why does fast move 2, not 3?" Any speed works for detection, but 2 guarantees no skipping and makes the start-finding math clean. 5.4
simple: Does following next pointers ever loop forever?

approaches.label: Brute Force (Hash Set)
steps: Walk the list, adding each node (the reference, not the value) to a set.
If a node is already in the set, return true. If we reach null, return false.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once with O(1) set operations; the set can hold all n nodes.
approaches.simple: Remember every node you visit in a set. Seeing one again means a loop.

approaches.label: Optimal (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare)
steps: slow = fast = head.
While fast and fast.next exist: slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next; if slow == fast return true.
Return false.
approaches.why: Fast reaches null in n/2 steps if no cycle; inside a cycle of length L the gap closes within L steps. Only two pointers are used.
approaches.simple: A slow walker moves 1 step and a fast runner moves 2. If there is a loop, the runner laps the walker and they meet.

title: Reorder List
problem: Given a list L0 -> L1 ->... -> Ln-1 -> Ln, reorder it in place to L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2 - >.... You may not change node values, only links. The function returns nothing.
example: Explanation: Take from the front, then the back, alternately.
intuition: We need to alternate between the front and the back. The front is easy to walk; the back is hard because a singly linked list cannot go backwards. Two fixes: copy nodes into an array (random access from both ends), or make the back half walkable forwards by reversing it.

So the optimal solution combines all three core moves: find the middle with slow/fast, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately. For 1 2 3 4 5: first half 1 2 3, second half 4 5 reversed to 5 4; weave: 1 5 2 4 3.
notes: Say it like this: "With an array of nodes I can two-pointer from both ends in O(n) time and O(n) space. To get O(1) space I split the list at the middle using slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, and weave the two halves together. Each step is linear, so O(n) time overall."
Edge cases: 0, 1 or 2 nodes (unchanged); odd vs even length (first half keeps the extra node).
Common mistakes: not cutting slow.next = null (creates a cycle); losing first.next before overwriting it; returning a value (the method is void).
Follow-ups: "Can you do it recursively?" Possible but O(n) stack. This three-step trick also solves Palindrome List (5.14). 5.5
simple: Reorder 1→2→3→4→5 into 1→5→2→4→3 (front, back, front, back…).

approaches.label: Brute Force (Array of Nodes)
steps: Store all nodes in an array.
Use two indices i = 0, j = n-1; link arr[i] -> arr[j] -> arr[i+1]... while moving inwards.
Set the last node's next to null.
approaches.why: One pass to fill the array and one to relink; the array stores n references.
approaches.simple: Put all nodes in an array and relink them using one index from each end.

approaches.label: Optimal (Middle, Reverse, Merge)
steps: Find the middle with slow/fast (fast starts at head.next so slow ends at the end of the first half).
Cut: second = slow.next, slow.next = null.
Reverse second.
Weave: take one from first, one from second, until second is empty.
approaches.why: Each of the three phases is a single linear pass; everything is done by relinking.
approaches.simple: Find the middle, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves together.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
pattern: Two pointers with a gap, dummy head
problem: Given the head of a linked list, remove the n-th node from the end and return the head. n is always valid (1 ≤ n ≤ length).
example: Explanation: The 2nd node from the end is 4; it is unlinked.
intuition: To delete a node we need the node before it. The n-th from the end is the (len - n + 1) -th from the start, so the simple way counts the length first. To do it in one pass, keep two pointers exactly n nodes apart: when the leading one reaches the last node, the trailing one is right before the target.
If the head itself is removed (n == length), there is no "node before". A dummy node in front of the head gives us one, so no special case is needed.
notes: Say it like this: "Two passes works: count the length, then walk to the node before position len-n+1, O(n) time O(1) space. In one pass I keep two pointers n apart starting from a dummy; when the front pointer is at the last node, the back pointer is just before the node to delete."
Edge cases: removing the head (n == length); single-node list (result is empty); removing the tail (n == 1).
Common mistakes: returning head instead of dummy.next (wrong when head is removed); off-by-one in the gap (gap n from dummy and stop at fast.next == null).
Follow-ups: "What if n can be larger than length?" Check fast for null while creating the gap and return head unchanged. 5.6
simple: Remove the n-th node counting from the end.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Two Passes)
steps: Count the length len.
From a dummy, walk len - n steps to reach the node before the target.
Skip the target: prev.next = prev.next.next. Return dummy.next.
approaches.why: Two linear passes, constant pointers. This is already fine; the follow-up asks for one pass.
approaches.simple: Count the length first, then walk to the node just before the one to delete.

approaches.label: Optimal (One Pass, Gap of n)
steps: fast = slow = dummy.
Move fast forward n steps.
Move both until fast.next == null. Now slow is just before the target.
slow.next = slow.next.next; return dummy.next.
approaches.why: fast traverses the list once and slow trails it; only pointers are stored.
approaches.simple: Move a fast pointer n steps ahead, then move both together. When fast reaches the end, slow is right before the node to delete.

title: Copy List With Random Pointer
pattern: Hash map of old to new / interleaving
problem: Each node has val, next, and random (which can point to any node or null). Build a deep copy: brand-new nodes whose next and random pointers mirror the original structure, with no pointer into the original list.
example: Explanation: Node 13's random points to node 7 (index 0), node 11's random to node 1 (index 4), etc.
intuition: Copying next is easy. The problem is random: when we copy node A whose random points to node X, the copy of X may not exist yet, and even if it does, how do we find it? We need a way to go from "original node" to "its copy".
A hash map original -> copy gives exactly that. Pass 1 creates all copies; pass 2 sets copy.next = map(orig.next) and copy.random = map(orig.random).

To avoid the map, store the mapping in the list itself: insert each copy right after its original (A -> A' -> B -> B'). Then the copy of any node X is simply X.next, so A'.random = A.random.next. Finally, unzip the two lists.
notes: Say it like this: "I need a mapping from each original node to its copy. With a hash map it's two passes: create copies, then wire next and random through the map, O(n) time and O(n) space. To get O(1) extra space I weave each copy right after its original so the copy of X is X.next, set randoms, then separate the lists."
Edge cases: empty list; random pointing to itself; random null; all randoms pointing to the same node.
Common mistakes: pointing a copy's random to an original node; not restoring the original list (the judge checks it); in the unzip, dereferencing copy.next.next when copy.next is null.
Follow-ups: "Clone a graph" (same map idea with DFS/BFS). "Can you do it in one pass with the map?" Yes: create copies lazily with getOrCreate for both next and random. 5.7
simple: Make a deep copy of a list where each node also has a random pointer.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Hash Map, Two Passes)
steps: Walk the list; for each node create a copy and store map.put(orig, copy).
Walk again; set copy.next = map.get(orig.next), copy.random = map.get(orig.random).
Return map.get(head).
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the map holds n entries. (The truly naive approach, finding each random target by walking from the head and counting its index, is O(n²); the map is the standard first answer.)
approaches.simple: First create a copy of every node in a map (old → new). Then fill in next and random using the map.

approaches.label: Optimal (Interleave Copies, O(1) Extra Space)
steps: For each node A, insert its copy A' right after it: A -> A' -> B -> B'....
For each original A: A.next.random = (A.random == null)? null: A.random.next.
Unzip: restore originals' next and link copies together. Return the first copy.
approaches.why: Three linear passes; apart from the output nodes, only a few pointers are used.
approaches.simple: Put each copy right after its original, set random pointers using that neighbour trick, then unzip the two lists.

title: Add Two Numbers
pattern: Digit-by-digit simulation with carry, dummy head
problem: Two non-negative integers are given as linked lists with digits in reverse order (head is the ones digit). Return their sum as a linked list in the same reverse format.
intuition: Reverse order is a gift: it is exactly the order we add numbers by hand, ones digit first. Add digit + digit + carry, write sum % 10, carry sum / 10 to the next position. Keep going while either list has digits or there is a carry left (e.g. 5 + 5 = 10 needs an extra node).
Converting to integers first looks easier but fails: lists can have up to 100 digits, far beyond long.
notes: Say it like this: "Converting to numbers overflows for long lists unless I use BigInteger. Instead I simulate school addition: walk both lists together adding digits plus carry, write sum mod 10, carry sum div 10, and continue while either list or the carry remains. O(max(n,m)) time, O(1) extra space."
Edge cases: different lengths; final carry (9 -> 9 + 1 = 0 -> 0 -> 1); both lists 0.
Common mistakes: forgetting the final carry; using sum / 10 in JS without Math.floor; converting to int / long (overflow).
Follow-ups: "Digits stored in forward order?" (LeetCode 445): reverse both lists first, or push digits onto two stacks, then add and build the result by prepending nodes. 5.8
simple: Add two numbers stored as linked lists of digits (in reverse order).

approaches.label: Brute Force (Convert to Numbers)
steps: Read each list into a big integer (digits are reversed, so multiply by increasing powers of 10).
Add them.
Write the sum back out digit by digit, ones digit first.
approaches.time: O(n + m) digit operations (BigInteger arithmetic adds some overhead)
approaches.why: Each digit is processed once; the big numbers and result list take linear space. With plain long this overflows beyond 18 digits, which is why we use BigInteger/BigInt.
approaches.simple: Turn each list into a real number, add them, and turn the result back into a list.

approaches.label: Optimal (Elementary Addition with Carry)
steps: dummy, tail, carry = 0.
While l1!= null || l2!= null || carry!= 0: sum = carry + (l1 digit or 0) + (l2 digit or 0).
Append sum % 10, set carry = sum / 10, advance the lists that are not finished.
Return dummy.next.
approaches.space: O(1) extra (output list is O(max(n, m)))
approaches.why: One step per digit position; aside from the result, only a carry and pointers.
approaches.simple: Add digit by digit like on paper, carrying 1 when a sum goes past 9.

title: Find The Duplicate Number
pattern: Floyd cycle detection on an implicit linked list
problem: An array nums of length n + 1 contains integers in the range [1, n]. Exactly one value repeats (possibly many times). Return that value without modifying the array and using only O(1) extra space.
example: Explanation: 2 appears twice; every value is between 1 and 4.
intuition: Why is this in the linked list section? Treat each index i as a node with an edge i -> nums[i]. Since every value is in [1, n], every edge points to a valid index, so starting from index 0 we can walk forever: there must be a cycle. Index 0 has no incoming edge (no value is 0), so it is the "head" outside the cycle.

The duplicate value d is an index with two incoming edges (two positions hold d). That is exactly the node where the tail joins the cycle, i.e. the cycle start. So: run Floyd's algorithm (5.15) on this implicit list.
Trace [1,3,4,2,2]: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 4 -> 2 -> 4... The cycle is 2 <-> 4 and it is entered at 2. Answer 2.
notes: Say it like this: "Comparing all pairs is O(n²); a hash set is O(n) time but O(n) space. Since values are in 1..n, I can view the array as a linked list i -> nums[i]. The duplicate has two incoming edges, so it's the start of the cycle, which Floyd's algorithm finds in O(n) time and O(1) space without modifying the array."
Edge cases: the duplicate appears more than twice (e.g. [2,2,2,2]); smallest input [1,1].
Common mistakes: starting phase 2 from nums[0] instead of 0; using a while instead of do-while in phase 1 (they start equal, so the loop never runs).

Follow-ups: "Binary search on value" is another O(n log n), O(1)-space answer: count elements ≤ mid; if count > mid, the duplicate is ≤ mid. Marking visited by negating nums[abs(x)] is O(n)/O(1) but modifies the array, which is not allowed here. 5.9
simple: An array has numbers 1..n with one number repeated. Find it without changing the array.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Compare Every Pair)
steps: For each i, for each j > i, if nums[i] == nums[j] return it.
approaches.why: All pairs are compared; no extra storage.
approaches.simple: Compare every pair.

approaches.label: Better (Hash Set or Sort)
steps: Walk the array with a set; the first value already in the set is the duplicate. (Sorting a copy and checking neighbours also works in O(n log n) time.)
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) set operations, but the set may hold n values, which breaks the O(1)-space rule.
approaches.simple: Use a set; the first number already in it is the duplicate.

approaches.label: Optimal (Floyd's Cycle Detection)
steps: Start slow = fast = 0 (index 0 is the head). Move slow = nums[slow] and fast = nums[nums[fast]] until they meet.
Reset slow = 0; move both one step at a time (x = nums[x]) until they meet.
The meeting point is the duplicate.
approaches.why: Floyd's algorithm takes linear steps on the n+1 implicit nodes; only two indices are stored and the array is untouched.
approaches.simple: Treat each value as a pointer to the next index. The duplicate creates a loop, and Floyd's tortoise and hare finds where the loop begins.

title: LRU Cache
problem: Design a Least Recently Used cache with a fixed capacity. get(key) returns the value or -1 if absent. put(key, value) inserts or updates; if this makes the cache exceed capacity, evict the least recently used key. Both operations must run in O(1) average time. Both get and put count as "using" a key.
example: Input:   LRUCache(2); put(1,1); put(2,2); get(1); put(3,3); get(2); put(4,4); get(1); get(3); get(4)
Output: null, null, null, 1, null, -1, null, -1, 3, 4
Explanation: After get(1), key 2 is least recent, so put(3,3) evicts 2. Then put(4,4) evicts 1.
intuition: We need two things fast: find a key (hash map, O(1)) and maintain an order of use where we can (a) move any key to "most recent" and (b) remove the "least recent" one, all in O(1).

An array or singly linked list cannot remove from the middle in O(1). A doubly linked list can, as long as we already hold the node: node.prev.next = node.next; node.next.prev = node.prev. So the map stores key -> node, and the list keeps nodes in recency order. Put the most recent right after a dummy head, and the least recent right before a dummy tail. Dummies remove all null checks.

get: look up node, move it to the front. put: if present, update value and move to front; otherwise create a node at the front, and if size exceeds capacity, remove tail.prev from both list and map (this is why the node stores its key).
notes: Say it like this: "A list kept in recency order works but makes get and put O(n). For O(1), I combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. The map finds the node in O(1), and the doubly linked list lets me unlink it and move it to the front, or drop the tail, in O(1). Dummy head and tail remove edge cases."
Edge cases: capacity 1; put on an existing key (update and refresh, no eviction); get on a missing key.

Common mistakes: not storing the key in the node (cannot remove from map on eviction); forgetting that get also refreshes recency; evicting before inserting when the key already exists; checking size before adding.

Follow-ups: "Thread safety?" Wrap operations with a lock (or synchronized), or use segment locks. "LFU cache?" (LeetCode 460): map key to node plus map frequency to a doubly linked list, and track the minimum frequency. 5.10
simple: Build a cache that, when full, throws out the item used longest ago.

approaches.label: Brute Force (List in Recency Order)
steps: Keep a list of [key, value] pairs ordered from least to most recent.
get: linear search; if found, remove it and append it at the end.
put: remove the existing pair if present, append the new pair, and if the size exceeds capacity remove index 0.
approaches.why: Searching and removing from the middle of a list are linear; storage is one entry per key.
approaches.simple: Keep items in a list ordered by recent use; move an item to the end when used and drop from the front when full.

approaches.label: Optimal (HashMap + Doubly Linked List)
steps: map: key -> node; doubly linked list with dummy head and tail; most recent after head.
get: if missing return -1; else unlink the node, insert it after head, return its value.
put: if present, update value and move to front. Else create a node, add to map and front; if map.size() > capacity, remove tail.prev from list and map.
approaches.why: Hash lookups are O(1) average and every list change touches a fixed number of pointers; we store one node and one map entry per key.
extra: Library shortcut (mention it, but expect to be asked to build the real thing): Java's LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true and an overridden removeEldestEntry, or in JS a Map (which keeps insertion order) where you delete and re- set a key on every use and evict map.keys().next().value.
approaches.simple: A map finds the node instantly; a doubly linked list keeps the order. Move a used node to the front and remove from the back when full.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
problem: You are given an array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge them all into one sorted linked list and return it.
example: Explanation: All nodes from the three lists in sorted order.
intuition: Let N be the total number of nodes. Merging two lists we already know (5.2). The question is how to combine k lists efficiently.

Merging one list at a time into a growing result re-walks the result again and again: O(k·N). Better ideas: (1) the next node of the answer is always the smallest of the k current heads, and a min-heap gives that in O(log k); (2) merge lists in pairs like merge sort: k lists become k/2, then k/4..., which is log k rounds of O(N) work each. Both give O(N log k).
notes: Say it like this: "Collecting and sorting is O(N log N). Merging lists one by one is O(kN) because the result is re- walked. With a min-heap holding the current head of each list, I always pop the global minimum in O(log k), giving O(N log k) time and O(k) space. Pairwise divide-and-conquer merging also gets O(N log k) with O(1) extra space."
Edge cases: lists empty; lists containing nulls; k = 1; all lists empty.
Common mistakes: pushing null heads into the heap; comparator overflow with a.val - b.val (use Integer.compare); in divide and conquer, wrong loop bounds that skip the last list.

Follow-ups: "Lists are too big for memory / streamed from k files?" The heap approach only needs k items in memory at a time, so it is the external-merge technique. "Kth smallest in a sorted matrix" uses the same heap- of-heads idea. 5.11
simple: Merge k sorted linked lists into one.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Collect and Sort)
steps: Put every value from every list into an array.
Sort it and build a new list.
approaches.why: Sorting all N values; the array and new nodes are linear.
approaches.simple: Collect every value, sort, and build a new list.

approaches.label: Better (Merge One by One)
steps: result = null.
For each list, result = mergeTwo(result, list).
approaches.why: The growing result is re-traversed for each of the k merges; merging only relinks nodes.
approaches.simple: Merge the lists one by one into a growing result.

approaches.label: Optimal (Min-Heap of Heads)
steps: Push the head of every non-empty list into a min-heap keyed by value.
Pop the smallest node, append it to the result, and push its next if not null.
Repeat until the heap is empty.
approaches.why: Each of the N nodes is pushed and popped once, each operation O(log k) because the heap never holds more than k nodes.
extra: Equally optimal and heap-free: divide and conquer. Merge lists in pairs (i with i + step), doubling step each round. There are log k rounds and each round touches all N nodes once: O(N log k) time, O(1) extra space. Handy in JavaScript.
approaches.simple: Keep the front node of every list in a min-heap. Take the smallest, then add that list's next node. (The second version merges lists in pairs, like merge sort.)

title: Reverse Nodes In K Group
problem: Given a linked list and an integer k, reverse the nodes in groups of k and return the new head. If the number of remaining nodes at the end is less than k, leave them as they are. Only links may change, not values.
example: Explanation: Groups [1,2] and [3,4] are reversed; [5] is shorter than k, so it stays.
intuition: This is "reverse a linked list" applied to segments, plus careful reconnection. For each group we need four references: the node before the group (groupPrev), the group's first node (which becomes its last), the group's last node kth (which becomes its first), and the node after the group (groupNext).

Algorithm per group: from groupPrev, walk k steps to find kth; if it doesn't exist, stop. Reverse the k nodes, but start prev at groupNext instead of null, so the reversed group's tail automatically links to the rest of the list. Then groupPrev.next = kth, and the old first node becomes the new groupPrev. A dummy before the head makes the first group identical to every other group.
notes: Say it like this: "Copying values to an array and reversing blocks is O(n) time and O(n) space but changes values. In place, I keep a pointer to the node before each group, check that k nodes exist, reverse those k nodes with prev initialised to the node after the group so the tail reconnects automatically, then hook the previous part to the new group head. O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: k = 1 (unchanged); k equal to length (full reversal); length not divisible by k (leftover stays); empty list.
Common mistakes: reversing the leftover partial group; losing groupNext; forgetting to move groupPrev to the old first node.
Follow-ups: "Reverse the leftover group too" (remove the length check). "Recursive version?" Reverse the first k nodes, then set oldHead.next = reverseKGroup(rest, k): O(n/k) stack. 5.12
simple: Reverse the list in blocks of k nodes; a short last block stays as it is.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Reverse Values via an Array)
steps: Copy all values into an array.
Reverse each full block of k inside the array.
Write values back into the nodes in order.
approaches.why: A constant number of passes over n values; the array holds all values. It changes values rather than links, which the problem forbids, so it is only a stepping stone.
approaches.simple: Copy values into an array, reverse each full block, and write them back.

approaches.label: Optimal (In-Place Group Reversal)
steps: dummy.next = head, groupPrev = dummy.
Find kth = k steps after groupPrev. If null, break.
groupNext = kth.next. Reverse from groupPrev.next with prev = groupNext, stopping at groupNext.
first = groupPrev.next (old first, now last); set groupPrev.next = kth; groupPrev = first. Repeat.
approaches.why: Each node is visited twice (once to find kth, once to reverse); only pointers are stored.
approaches.simple: For each group, find its k-th node, reverse the arrows inside the group, and stitch it back between the previous and next groups.

title: Find Middle of Linked List
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, return its middle node. If there are two middle nodes (even length), return the second one (LeetCode 876).
example: Explanation: Middles are 3 and 4; we return the second one.
intuition: The obvious way: count the nodes, then walk count / 2 steps. In one pass: if fast moves twice as fast as slow, then when fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the distance, so it stands at the middle.

Which middle you get depends on the loop condition. With while (fast!= null && fast.next!= null) starting both at head, slow lands on the second middle. Starting fast = head.next gives the first middle (used in 5.4 and 5.19 to split a list).
notes: Say it like this: "I can count the nodes and walk n/2 steps, which is O(n) with two passes. In one pass I use slow and fast pointers: fast moves two steps per one step of slow, so when fast hits the end, slow is at the middle. O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: single node (return it); two nodes (return the second).
Common mistakes: confusing first vs second middle; checking only fast.next and crashing when fast is null.
Follow-ups: "Return the first middle" (start fast = head.next). "Delete the middle node" (LeetCode 2095): start fast = head.next.next so slow stops one before the middle. 5.13
simple: Find the middle node (the second middle if there are two).

approaches.label: Brute Force (Count, Then Walk)
steps: Count the length n.
Walk n / 2 steps from the head and return that node.
approaches.why: About 1.5 passes over the list; two variables.
approaches.simple: Count the nodes, then walk half that many steps.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tortoise and Hare)
steps: slow = fast = head.
While fast!= null && fast.next!= null: slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next.
Return slow.
approaches.why: fast crosses the list once (n/2 iterations); two pointers only.
approaches.simple: Slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2. When fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle.

title: Find the intersection point of Y LL
problem: Two singly linked lists may merge at some node and share all nodes after it, forming a "Y" shape. Return the node where they intersect, or null if they never meet (LeetCode 160, Intersection of Two Linked Lists). The lists have no cycles and must keep their original structure.
example: Input:   listA = 4 -> 1 -> 8 -> 4 -> 5, listB = 5 -> 6 -> 1 -> 8 -> 4 -> 5 (the 8 node is shared)
Explanation: From node 8 onwards both lists use the very same nodes. Note the 1s are different nodes.
intuition: Intersection means the same node object, not equal values. After the meeting point, both lists share an identical tail. The only difference is the length of the parts before the meeting point.

If A's private part has length a, B's private part b, and the shared tail c, then a pointer that walks A then B covers a + c + b steps before reaching the junction the second time, and a pointer that walks B then A covers b + c + a. Same distance! So walk both pointers, and when one hits the end, send it to the other list's head. They meet at the junction, or both become null together if there is no junction (both covered a + b).
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force compares every pair of nodes, O(n·m). A hash set of A's nodes gives O(n+m) time but O(n) space. For O(1) space, I run two pointers and redirect each to the other list's head when it reaches the end; both then travel the same total distance and meet at the junction, or both reach null."
Edge cases: no intersection (return null; loop ends when both are null); one list empty; intersection at the very first node; one list is a suffix of the other.
Common mistakes: comparing values instead of references; redirecting on p.next == null instead of p == null (infinite loop when there is no intersection).

Follow-ups: "What if the lists can have cycles?" Find each list's cycle start first (5.15) and reason case by case. "Can you modify the lists?" Then you could temporarily connect A's tail to B's head and find the cycle start, then undo. 5.14
simple: Two lists merge into one shared tail, like a Y. Find the first shared node.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Check Every Pair)
steps: For each node of A, walk the whole of B looking for the same node.
approaches.why: Every node of A is compared against every node of B.
approaches.simple: For each node of A, scan all of B for the same node.

approaches.label: Better (Hash Set)
steps: Put every node of A in a set.
Walk B; the first node found in the set is the intersection.
approaches.why: One pass over each list; the set stores all nodes of A.
approaches.simple: Put all nodes of A in a set; walk B until you hit one.

approaches.label: Optimal (Switch Heads)
steps: p = headA, q = headB.
While p!= q: p = (p == null)? headB: p.next; q = (q == null)? headA: q.next.
Return p (the junction or null).
approaches.why: Each pointer walks at most n + m nodes before they meet; two pointers only.
extra: An equivalent O(1)-space method that is easier to explain under pressure: compute both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference, then move both together until they are the same node.
approaches.simple: Two walkers; when one reaches the end, it jumps to the other list's head. Both walk the same total distance, so they meet at the shared node.

title: Check if LL is palindrome or not
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if its values read the same forwards and backwards (LeetCode 234, Palindrome Linked List). Aim for O(n) time and O(1) space.
example: Explanation: Reading backwards gives 1 2 2 1, the same sequence.
intuition: A palindrome check needs to compare the first value with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on. With an array that is trivial. Without extra space, the problem is again that we cannot walk backwards, so (as in 5.4) we reverse the second half: then walking the first half and the reversed second half side by side compares exactly the mirror pairs.
Good practice (and a point interviewers like): reverse the second half back afterwards, so the input is unchanged.
notes: Say it like this: "Copying values to an array and checking with two pointers is O(n) time and O(n) space. For O(1) space I find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half, compare it against the first half, and then reverse it back to restore the list. Still O(n) time."
Edge cases: empty or single node (true); two nodes; odd length (the middle node needs no partner).

Common mistakes: comparing Integer objects with!= in Java (fails above 127, use primitives or equals); not restoring the list; looping on p1 instead of p2 and comparing the middle element against null.

Follow-ups: "Is modifying the input acceptable?" Say you restore it; in a concurrent setting you would prefer the O(n) space version. A recursive solution (compare on the way back from recursion) exists but uses O(n) stack. 5.15
simple: Does the list read the same forwards and backwards?

approaches.label: Brute Force (Copy to an Array)
steps: Copy all values to an array (or push onto a stack).
Two pointers from both ends; any mismatch means false.
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the array holds n values.
approaches.simple: Copy the values into an array and compare from both ends.

approaches.label: Optimal (Reverse Second Half)
steps: Find the end of the first half with slow/fast, looping while fast.next!= null && fast.next.next!= null.
Reverse the list after slow.
Compare the first half with the reversed second half node by node.
Reverse the second half back and reconnect; return the result.
approaches.why: Find middle, reverse, compare and restore are each linear; only pointers are used.
approaches.simple: Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare the halves, then reverse it back.

title: Find the starting point in LL
problem: Given the head of a linked list, return the node where the cycle begins, or null if there is no cycle (LeetCode 142, Linked List Cycle II). Do not modify the list.
example: Input:   head = 3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4, and -4.next points back to node 2
Explanation: Node 2 is the first node that is visited twice.
intuition: With a hash set, the first node we see twice is the cycle start. For O(1) space, use Floyd's algorithm in two phases.

Phase 1: slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps) meet somewhere inside the cycle. Let L = distance from head to cycle start, C = cycle length, x = distance from cycle start to meeting point. When they meet, slow walked L + x, fast walked 2(L + x), and fast's extra distance L + x is a whole number of loops: L + x = kC. So L = kC - x: walking L steps from the meeting point lands exactly on the cycle start (it finishes the current loop and maybe some full loops).
Phase 2: put one pointer at head and keep one at the meeting point; move both one step at a time. After L steps both are at the cycle start, so the node where they meet is the answer.
notes: Say it like this: "A hash set returns the first repeated node in O(n) time and O(n) space. With Floyd's algorithm, slow and fast first meet inside the loop; the math L + x = kC shows the distance from head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point forward to the start, so moving one pointer from head and one from the meeting point in lockstep makes them meet at the start. O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: no cycle; cycle starting at the head; self-loop on a single node.
Common mistakes: starting phase 2 from head.next or moving fast 2 steps in phase 2; being unable to justify why it works (practise the L + x = kC derivation).

Follow-ups: "Cycle length?" (5.16). "Find duplicate number" (5.8) is this exact algorithm on an array. "Remove the cycle?" Find the start, then walk around the loop to the node whose next is the start and set its next to null. 5.16
simple: If the list loops, find the node where the loop starts.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Hash Set)
steps: Walk the list adding nodes to a set.
The first node already in the set is the cycle start; reaching null means no cycle.
approaches.why: Each node is inserted once; the set may hold all n nodes.
approaches.simple: The first node you visit twice is the start.

approaches.label: Optimal (Floyd, Two Phases)
steps: Move slow 1 and fast 2 until they meet; if fast reaches null, return null.
Set p = head; move p and slow one step at a time until p == slow.
Return p.
approaches.why: Phase 1 takes at most about L + C steps and phase 2 exactly L steps; two pointers only.
approaches.simple: Let slow and fast meet inside the loop. Then walk one pointer from the head and one from the meeting point at the same speed; they meet at the loop's start.

title: Length of loop in LL
problem: Given the head of a linked list, return the number of nodes in its loop, or 0 if there is no loop (GFG "Find length of Loop"; not on LeetCode, so we use a method countNodesInLoop(ListNode head) on the standard ListNode).
example: Input:   head = 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, and 5.next points back to node 2
Explanation: The loop is 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 2, which contains 4 nodes.
intuition: If we remember the position (step number) at which each node was first visited, then the moment we visit a node again, the loop length is current step - first step for that node.
Without memory: once slow and fast meet, we know we are inside the loop. Freeze one pointer and walk the other around until it returns; the number of steps is the loop length.
notes: Say it like this: "Storing the step at which each node was first seen gives the loop length as the difference when a node repeats, O(n) time and O(n) space. With Floyd's algorithm I detect a meeting point inside the loop and then walk around once, counting nodes, for O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: no loop (0); self-loop (1); whole list is a loop (n).
Common mistakes: starting the count at 0 and walking from slow itself (loop exits immediately); counting from the head instead of from inside the loop.
Follow-ups: "Use the length to find the start": move one pointer C steps ahead from the head, then move both together; they meet at the start. 5.17
simple: Count how many nodes are inside the loop.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Hash Map of Positions)
steps: Walk the list with a counter pos, storing node -> pos.
If the current node is already in the map, return pos - map.get(node).
If we reach null, return 0.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; the map holds up to n entries.
approaches.simple: Remember the step number of each node. When you meet a node again, the difference in step numbers is the loop length.

approaches.label: Optimal (Floyd, Then Walk the Loop)
steps: Run slow/fast until they meet; if fast reaches null, return 0.
From the meeting node, move a pointer forward counting steps until it returns to the meeting node.
Return the count.
approaches.why: Detection is linear and the counting walk is exactly C ≤ n steps; only pointers and a counter.
approaches.simple: Find a meeting point with slow/fast, then walk around the loop once counting steps.

title: Sort a Linked List of 0's 1's and 2's
problem: Given a linked list whose node values are only 0, 1 or 2, rearrange it so all 0s come first, then 1s, then 2s, and return the new head (GFG "Sort a linked list of 0s, 1s and 2s"; not on LeetCode, so we use sortList012(ListNode head) on the standard ListNode). Prefer relinking nodes over changing values.
example: Explanation: One 0, two 1s and five 2s, in that order.
intuition: There are only three possible values, so we do not need a general sort. Counting how many 0s, 1s and 2s exist and rewriting values works in two passes. But if nodes carry other data, rewriting values is wrong; we should move the nodes.

Moving nodes is easy with dummies: keep three separate lists (zeros, ones, twos), each with its own dummy head and tail. Walk the original list once, appending each node to the matching list. Finally connect zeros -> ones -> twos, being careful when a list is empty, and terminate the last node with null.
notes: Say it like this: "Copying and sorting is O(n log n). Counting 0s, 1s and 2s and overwriting values is O(n) and O(1) space but changes data. The cleanest is one pass that moves each node into one of three dummy-headed lists, then joins them, still O(n) time and O(1) space, and it keeps node identity."
Edge cases: empty list; all nodes the same value; one of the three groups missing (e.g. no 1s).
Common mistakes: forgetting t.next = null (the old link can create a cycle); linking z.next = oneD.next when the ones list is empty (drops the twos).
Follow-ups: "Partition List" (LeetCode 86, nodes < x before nodes ≥ x) is the same two-dummy technique. "Odd Even Linked List" (LeetCode 328) too. 5.18
simple: Sort a linked list that only has 0s, 1s and 2s.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Copy, Sort, Write Back)
steps: Copy all values into an array.
Sort the array.
Overwrite node values in order.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the array holds n values.
approaches.simple: Copy values, sort, and write them back.

approaches.label: Better (Count and Overwrite)
steps: Count the 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass.
In a second pass, write count0 zeros, then count1 ones, then the 2s into the nodes.
approaches.why: Two linear passes and three counters. Downside: it rewrites values instead of moving nodes.
approaches.simple: Count 0s, 1s and 2s, then overwrite the values in order.

approaches.label: Optimal (Three Lists, Relink Nodes)
steps: Create dummies zeroD, oneD, twoD with tails z, o, t.
Walk the list; append each node to the tail matching its value.
Connect: z.next = (oneD.next!= null)? oneD.next: twoD.next; o.next = twoD.next; t.next = null.
Return zeroD.next.
approaches.why: A single pass with a fixed number of dummy nodes and pointers; nodes are moved, values untouched.
extra: Note the return line: if there are no zeros, zeroD.next is the ones list (step 3 linked it), so zeroD.next alone is actually enough; the fallback just makes the intent obvious.
approaches.simple: Make three small lists (zeros, ones, twos), move each node into the right one, then join the three lists.

title: Rotate a LL
problem: Given the head of a linked list, rotate the list to the right by k places and return the new head (LeetCode 61, Rotate List). k can be much larger than the length.
intuition: Rotating right by 1 moves the tail to the front. Rotating by n (the length) gives back the same list, so only k % n matters; that saves us when k is 2 billion.

Rotating by k means the last k nodes move to the front. The new tail is the node at position n - k (1-based), and the new head is the one after it. Neat trick: connect the old tail to the head (making a circle), walk n - k steps to the new tail, and cut the circle there.
notes: Say it like this: "Rotating one step at a time costs O(n) per step, O(n·k) overall. Since rotating by n is a no-op, I use k mod n, then connect the tail to the head and cut the ring after the (n-k)-th node. That's O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: empty list; single node; k = 0; k a multiple of n; k much larger than n.
Common mistakes: not taking k % n (time limit or wrong answer); forgetting to break the ring (infinite list); off-by-one in n - k - 1 steps.
Follow-ups: "Rotate left by k?" Same as rotating right by n - k % n. "Rotate an array" (LeetCode 189): reverse whole, then reverse the two parts. 5.19
simple: Rotate the list to the right by k places.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Rotate One Step at a Time)
steps: Compute n and reduce k = k % n (without this, k up to 2·10⁹ would time out).
Repeat k times: walk to the second-last node, detach the tail and put it in front.
approaches.time: O(n·k), which is O(n²) after the modulo
approaches.why: Each single rotation walks the whole list; only pointers are used.
approaches.simple: Move the last node to the front, k times.

approaches.label: Optimal (Close the Ring, Cut Once)
steps: Walk to the tail while counting n.
k %= n; if k == 0 return head.
tail.next = head (make a circle).
Walk n - k - 1 steps from the head to reach the new tail (the node at position n - k).
newHead = newTail.next, newTail.next = null. Return newHead.
approaches.why: At most two passes over the list; a few pointers.
approaches.simple: Connect the tail to the head to make a ring, then cut the ring at the right spot.

title: Sort LL
pattern: Merge sort on a linked list
problem: Given the head of a linked list, return the list sorted in ascending order (LeetCode 148, Sort List). The follow-up asks for O(n log n) time and O(1) memory.
example: Explanation: Standard ascending sort of the node values.
intuition: Which sort suits a linked list? Quick sort and heap sort need random access. Merge sort only needs: split in half (slow/fast pointers), sort each half recursively, and merge two sorted lists (5.2). Merging lists needs no extra array, unlike merging arrays. So merge sort is the natural O(n log n) choice and combines two of our core moves.
To split, use the "first middle" version (fast = head.next) so that a 2-node list splits into 1 + 1; with the second- middle version it would split into 2 + 0 and recurse forever.
notes: Say it like this: "Copying values to an array and sorting is O(n log n) time but O(n) space. Merge sort fits linked lists perfectly: split with slow/fast pointers, sort halves recursively, and merge without extra arrays. That's O(n log n) time and O(log n) recursion space; bottom-up merge sort brings space to O(1)."
Edge cases: empty list; one node; already sorted; all equal values; negative values.
Common mistakes: using the second-middle split (infinite recursion on 2 nodes); forgetting slow.next = null; JS sort() without a comparator sorts as strings.
Follow-ups: "Why not quick sort?" Worst case O(n²) and partitioning is awkward without random access. "Insertion Sort List" (LeetCode 147) is the O(n²) alternative. 5.20
simple: Sort a linked list.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Array Sort, Write Back)
steps: Copy values into an array.
Sort it.
Write values back into the nodes.
approaches.why: Sorting the array; the array stores n values.
approaches.simple: Copy values into an array, sort it, write them back.

approaches.label: Optimal (Top-Down Merge Sort)
steps: Base case: 0 or 1 node, return it.
Find the end of the first half with slow = head, fast = head.next; cut mid = slow.next; slow.next = null.
Recursively sort both halves.
Merge the two sorted halves with a dummy head.
approaches.why: log n levels of splitting, and each level does O(n) total work for finding middles and merging. The only extra memory is the recursion stack of depth log n.
extra: For strict O(1) space, a bottom-up merge sort merges runs of size 1, 2, 4,... iteratively without recursion. It is longer to code; mention it, and write it only if asked.
approaches.simple: Merge sort: split the list in the middle, sort each half, merge the two sorted halves.

title: Flattening of LL
problem: Each node has a next pointer (to the next "column" head) and a bottom pointer (down its own column). Every column, read through bottom, is sorted. Flatten everything into a single sorted list linked only through bottom (all next pointers null) and return its head (GFG "Flattening a Linked List"; not on LeetCode). Here the node class is Node { int data; Node next, bottom; }.
example: Explanation: All 13 values in sorted order in one bottom-linked list.
intuition: This is Merge K Sorted Lists (5.10) in disguise: each column is a sorted list, and the next pointers just tell us where the columns start. Anything that merges k sorted lists works. The classic expected answer is recursive: flatten everything to the right of the current column, then merge the current column with that result (merging via bottom). Merging from the right means each merge only deals with two sorted lists. For the fastest version, use a min-heap of column heads exactly as in 5.10.
notes: Say it like this: "This is merge k sorted lists. Collecting and sorting is O(N log N) time and O(N) space. The standard answer recursively flattens the right part and merges it with the current column via bottom pointers, using only recursion stack. A min-heap of column heads is the fastest at O(N log k) time and O(k) space."
Edge cases: null root; a single column (already sorted, but clear next); columns of length 1.
Common mistakes: merging through next instead of bottom; leaving next pointers set (GFG's checker may follow them); polling a node and pushing its bottom after you have overwritten node.bottom.

Follow-ups: "Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List" (LeetCode 430) is a different problem: preserve order (not sort) using DFS and a stack. "Do it iteratively?" Merge columns left to right with a loop instead of recursion.
simple: Columns of sorted lists hang from a top row. Flatten everything into one sorted list using the bottom pointers.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Collect, Sort, Rebuild)
steps: Walk every column and every node, collecting all values.
Sort them.
Build a new list linked through bottom.
approaches.why: N = total nodes; sorting dominates and the array plus new nodes take linear space.
approaches.simple: Collect all values, sort them, and build a new list.

approaches.label: Better (Recursive Merge from the Right)
steps: If root is null or has no next, return it.
rest = flatten(root.next).
Return merge(root, rest), where merge joins two bottom-sorted lists and sets every next to null.
approaches.time: O(N·k) in the worst case, k = number of columns
approaches.why: Each merge re-walks the already merged suffix, like merging one by one in 5.10; recursion depth equals the number of columns. Compared to Approach 1 it uses no array and relinks the original nodes, which is why it is the standard interview answer.
approaches.simple: Flatten the columns from the right, merging each column into the already-flattened rest.

approaches.label: Optimal (Min-Heap of Column Heads)
steps: Push every column head into a min-heap by data.
Pop the smallest node, append it via bottom, clear its next, and push its bottom if non-null.
Repeat until the heap is empty.
approaches.why: Every node passes through the heap once with O(log k) cost; the heap holds at most one node per column.
approaches.simple: Keep each column's current top node in a min-heap and repeatedly take the smallest.
